newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South African trade unions turn capitalist.
newsitem.headline: South African trade unions turn capitalist.

text.p: In smoke-filled rooms South African trade unionists are busy becoming good capitalists, gaining access to levers of economic power in ways undreamt of a few years ago.

Last week a group of 23 black groups, dominated by the unions, pulled in 2.7 billion rand ($580 million) for a controlling 35 percent stake in leading conglomerate Johnnies Industrial Corp Ltd (Johnnic).

At one stage the deal was hanging in the balance as the disparate grouping struggled to raise funds to buy the prestigious chunk of corporate South Africa from Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd.
In the event, the offer was oversubscribed by 20 percent.

"That it has been oversubscribed by 20 percent is evidence of the support...for black empowerment," chief negotiator Cyril Ramaphosa, the one-time union leader who led a crippling miners' strike in 1987, declared at the weekend.

Ramaphosa's old union, the National Union of Mineworkers (NUM), walked off with the lion's share of the 35 percent stake, representing 4.5 percent of Johnnic's equity. Combined with the shares held by the NUM's investment company, the stake is 5.8 percent.
Ramaphosa himself is set to secure the chairmanship of Johnnic when the company's reconstituted board, dominated by the black National Empowerment Consortium (NEC), convenes in a few weeks time.

The Johnnic sale, easily the biggest empowerment deal to date, gives blacks control or influence over companies representing nearly 10 percent of the capitalisation of the Johannesburg Stock Exchange.
Johnnic's assets include stakes in South African Breweries Ltd, Premier Group Ltd, insurance and media companies.
There is no doubt the NEC has got a bargain.
Anglo, keen to demonstrate its commitment to black advancement, is selling its shares in Johnnic for 50 rand each, while the stock was trading on Monday at 55 rand.
The question is how the NEC will exploit its new powerbase.
Leading bankers say Ramaphosa and his allies will likely use their position to open doors to other deals, which might lead to the transfer of more valuable assets in future.
High on black business' wish list is JCI Ltd, the country's sixth-biggest mining concern and another Anglo- controlled company which it aims to hive off to black owners.
Ramaphosa is also keen to use the new union-backed alliance as a springboard into privatisation deals.

In the political corridors of power the debate is raging between labour and government on the sale of state assets -- but if shares are going to be sold, unions are keen to get a slice of the action for their members.

Nthato Motlana, chairman of South Africa's largest black listed company, New Africa Investments Ltd, believes the new streak of capitalism in the union movement can help transform old confrontational attitudes.

"I am happy the unions are involved in business. They will realise that you pay workers out of profits, not out of capital, and then hopefully the strikes and industrial action will decrease," he told the Sunday Independent.
